gara-tie-dye.intro: Learn Gara tie-dyeing from the ground up — from understanding cotton and indigo to running a workshop that exports. Master the craft, then build a business around it.

skillDomains.name: Materials & Fabric
skillDomains.description: Know your materials. Fabric choice, thread, and tool handling determine everything downstream.

skills.name: Fabric Fundamentals
skills.description: Identify cotton types, weaves, and how each takes dye.

modules.title: What is Gara?
modules.content:
Gara is the Sierra Leonean name for wax-resist and tie-dye textiles. It shares roots with Nigerian adire and sits inside the wider West African resist-dye tradition.

The technique is simple to say and hard to master: you prevent dye from reaching parts of the cloth, then dye the rest. The untouched parts stay pale. The dyed parts go deep.

Gara is not decoration. It is a language. Every pattern has a name, a history, and a message.

By the end of this skill, you will look at any cloth and know what it is, how it was made, and what it can become.

modules.title: Cotton, rayon, silk — how they differ
modules.content:
Cotton

The traditional base for Gara. Absorbs dye evenly. Durable. Locally available. Start here.

Rayon

Takes dye brighter than cotton but fades faster and can tear under heavy handling. Use for decorative cloth, not for wearables.

Silk

Luxury-grade. Rare in West African workshops because of cost. Produces stunning colour depth.

The rule

If you can only buy one fabric for your whole learning journey: 100% cotton. It forgives mistakes and rewards skill.

steps.q: Which fabric is best for a Gara cloth that must last years and be worn regularly?
steps.f: Cotton holds dye and lasts. Synthetics resist dye or fade unevenly.

steps.q: You feel a fabric that is cool, slightly rough, and when burned turns to soft ash with a paper smell. What is it?
steps.f: The burn test — natural fibres turn to ash and smell like burnt paper; synthetics melt into a hard bead.

steps.q: Which fabric takes dye the brightest but fades fastest?
steps.f: Rayon absorbs dye fast and bright but loses colour quickly under sun and washing.

modules.title: Why you must wash before dyeing
modules.content:
New fabric has sizing — a starch coating added during manufacturing to keep it crisp. Sizing blocks dye. If you dye new cloth without washing, you get uneven, pale results.

The prep routine

  1. Fill a basin with hot water and a spoon of detergent.
  2. Soak the fabric for 30 minutes.
  3. Rinse in clean water until no suds remain.
  4. Hang to dry — do not tumble.
  5. Iron flat before marking patterns.
Prep is 30% of the finished quality. Skip it and every later step fights you.

steps.q: You have just bought new cotton from the market. What is the very first step?
o: Wash in hot water with detergent
steps.f: Always wash first. Everything else comes after.

steps.q: After washing, the fabric is dry but wrinkled. What do you do before marking patterns?
steps.f: Wrinkles distort pattern marks. Iron flat while dry.

steps.q: You wash in cold water only. What is the risk?
steps.f: Cold water does not fully remove sizing. Hot water and detergent are required.

modules.title: Customer wants a low-shrink cloth
modules.prompt: A customer commissions a 2-metre Gara cloth and insists it must not shrink more than 2% after washing. Raw cotton shrinks 5–10% on first wash. You have the tools and time to pre-treat. How do you prepare the fabric?
modules.context: This is a real commercial concern — export clients will reject orders that shrink beyond spec.
modules.placeholder: Describe your preparation steps in order…
rubric: Pre-wash before cutting to size
Note the expected shrink percentage
Describe how you dry (line vs tumble)
Confirm final measurement check after drying
Address any additional stabilisation step (e.g., hot wash + cold rinse)

modules.title: Write your fabric prep SOP
modules.prompt: Create a one-page Standard Operating Procedure for preparing fabric before dyeing, usable by any workshop apprentice.
modules.context: Real workshops run on written procedures. This becomes part of your professional portfolio.
steps: List each step with clear instructions
Note equipment needed for each step
Include a quality checkpoint after each step
Add a photo or sketch of the setup

skills.name: Threads & Tools
skills.description: The needles, threads, waxes, and tools you work with every day.

modules.title: The thread matters
modules.content:
In tie-dye Gara, thread is not for sewing — it is your drawing tool. The way you tie and stitch determines the pattern.

Common threads

  • Cotton twine — strong, forgiving, works for thick folds
  • Nylon thread — thin, precise, for fine pattern work
  • Rubber bands — quick and cheap, good for beginners

Professional Gara makers keep a range of thicknesses on hand. Thin thread makes fine lines; thick thread makes bold ones.

modules.title: Your workshop toolkit
modules.content:
A serious Gara workshop needs:

  • Sharp scissors
  • Needles in multiple sizes
  • Wooden pegs or clamps
  • A large dye pot (enamel or stainless steel — never aluminium)
  • Wooden stirring stick dedicated to dye
  • Rubber gloves
  • A drying line in shade

The dye pot is the most important. Aluminium reacts with indigo and ruins the bath. Enamel or stainless steel lasts for years.

modules.title: Match the tool to its job

steps.q: You need to make fine, precise lines in a small pattern. Which tool?
steps.f: Nylon thread is thin and precise — perfect for fine lines.

steps.q: Which material must your dye pot NOT be made of?
steps.f: Aluminium reacts with indigo and metallic salts, ruining the bath.

steps.q: You're dyeing a large cloth and need to keep folds tight for a bold pattern. Best option?
steps.f: Rubber bands or heavy twine hold thick folds tightly under dye pressure.

modules.title: Three foundational tie techniques
modules.content:
1. Spiral tie

Lay the fabric flat, pinch the centre, and twist. Tie at intervals along the twist. Creates a radiating spiral pattern.

2. Fold-and-tie

Fold the fabric into a triangle or strip, then tie across the fold at regular intervals. Creates repeating geometric bands.

3. Stitch-and-gather

Run a needle and thread along a marked line, then gather tightly. Creates long, flowing lines that follow the stitching.

Practice each on a small square before applying to a full cloth.

steps.q: You want a repeating geometric band pattern across the cloth.
steps.f: Fold-and-tie creates clean repeating bands.

steps.q: You want a radiating sunburst from the centre.
steps.f: Spiral tie is the only technique that produces a radiating sunburst.

steps.q: You want long, flowing lines following a curve you've drawn.
steps.f: Stitch-and-gather follows any line you can stitch, no matter the shape.

modules.title: Build a tie-technique sampler
modules.prompt: Create a sampler of at least 5 distinct tie techniques on small fabric squares. Photograph and label each one with the technique, thread used, and expected result.
steps: Cut 5+ squares of washed cotton
Apply a different technique to each
Dye them all in the same bath for consistency
Photograph the finished sampler
Write a one-line note under each about what you learned

skills.name: Workshop Safety
skills.description: Protect your hands, lungs, and workspace. Dye work involves chemicals and dyes that demand respect.

modules.title: Why safety is a skill
modules.content:
Indigo, caustic soda, and dye fixatives are powerful chemicals. A workshop that ignores safety will eventually injure someone — usually the youngest apprentice.

Safety is not optional. It is a core professional skill. Every professional workshop you visit will have safety protocols. Learning them now is how you become employable later.

modules.title: Personal protective equipment
modules.content:
Always wear

  • Rubber gloves — caustic soda burns skin
  • Apron or old clothes — dye stains permanently
  • Closed shoes — spills happen
  • Dust mask — when handling powdered dyes

Never do

  • Eat or drink in the dye area
  • Touch your face with gloved hands
  • Work alone with caustic soda on a first attempt

steps.q: You're about to mix caustic soda into water. Which is correct?
o: Add soda to water slowly while stirring
steps.f: Always add caustic soda to water, never the reverse.

steps.q: You must handle powdered dye. What PPE is essential?
steps.f: Powdered dye can be inhaled. Mask and gloves are minimum.

steps.q: You finish dyeing and your gloves have dye on them. What do you do?
o: Rinse them in the dye pot
Peel them off by the cuff and dispose safely
steps.f: Peel gloves from the cuff inward without touching the outside.

modules.title: Handle a chemical splash
modules.prompt: An apprentice spills caustic soda solution on their forearm. They are panicking. You are the workshop lead. Walk through exactly what you do in order.
modules.context: Caustic soda burns continue until thoroughly flushed. Fast, correct action prevents scarring.
rubric: Remove contaminated clothing/gloves first
Flush with copious running water for at least 20 minutes
Do NOT neutralise with acid — flushing is the correct response
Do NOT apply creams or ointments
Arrange medical assessment
Record the incident for future prevention

modules.title: Write a workshop safety code
modules.prompt: You are opening a small Gara workshop with three apprentices. Write a one-page safety code that covers daily operations.
modules.context: Insurance, government registration, and export contracts increasingly require documented safety procedures.
rubric: Covers PPE requirements
Covers chemical handling and storage
Covers emergency procedures
Assigns responsibility (who checks what, when)
Includes a training requirement for new apprentices

modules.title: Design a workshop safety poster
modules.prompt: Design and photograph a safety poster to display in your workshop. It must be readable from 2 metres and cover the four most important safety rules.
steps: Choose the 4 most important rules
Design with clear icons and short text
Use colours that stand out
Print or hand-paint and display in your workspace
Photograph the finished poster in place

skillDomains.name: Design & Pattern
skillDomains.description: Design is what separates a craftsperson from an artist. Learn to plan patterns with intention and cultural awareness.

skills.name: Pattern Design
skills.description: Plan, sketch, and predict how patterns will look after dyeing.

modules.title: Pattern is intention
modules.content:
Every strong Gara cloth starts on paper. Not in dye.

Professional pattern design has four steps:

  1. Intention — what is this cloth for? Wearable? Wall art? Commission?
  2. Sketch — draw the layout on paper.
  3. Predict — imagine what each mark will become after dye and resist.
  4. Test — cut a small sample square and dye it before committing the full cloth.

Beginners skip the sketch and regret it. Professionals always sketch.

modules.title: Predicting the result
modules.content:
In dyeing, what you tie stays pale; what you don't goes dark. Beginners picture the opposite.

Before you tie a single knot, ask:

  • Which parts will resist dye?
  • Which parts will absorb it fully?
  • What happens at the boundary — will it be sharp or feathered?

Sharp boundaries come from tight wrapping. Feathered boundaries come from looser ties. Both are useful. Know which you want.

steps.q: You tie tightly at 5 evenly spaced points along a folded strip, then dye. What pattern appears?
steps.f: Evenly spaced ties produce evenly spaced pale bands.

steps.q: You tie loosely with thin thread. The dye bleeds slightly into the resisted area. What boundary do you get?
steps.f: Loose ties allow dye to creep in, producing a soft feathered edge.

steps.q: You want a full-coverage pattern with no visible pale areas. What approach?
o: Tie many points densely across the whole cloth
steps.f: Dense multi-point tying is how you build a busy, full-coverage pattern.

modules.title: Design for a client brief
modules.prompt: A boutique in Freetown commissions 10 Gara scarves for a spring collection. Brief: bold geometric patterns, indigo and natural white, suitable for office wear. Describe your design approach — layout, technique, colours, and how you'll test before production.
modules.context: Professional design work always responds to a brief.
rubric: References the brief (bold geometric, indigo + white, office-appropriate)
Chooses specific tie techniques that produce geometric patterns
Considers consistency across a 10-piece run
Describes a sample-test step before committing to production
Addresses production time and material estimate

modules.title: Build a pattern design portfolio
modules.prompt: Create a portfolio of at least 4 original pattern designs, each with a sketch, a sample, and a one-paragraph note explaining the intention.
steps: Sketch each pattern on paper
Produce a physical sample
Photograph sketch and sample together
Write a note: what was the intention? What worked? What would you change?
Assemble into a single portfolio document

skills.name: Cultural Symbols
skills.description: Understand the meaning behind West African patterns. Gara is not decoration — it is a language.

modules.title: Patterns carry meaning
modules.content:
Throughout West Africa, textile patterns carry meaning — proverbs, historical events, values, social status, and identity. A client commissioning a cloth for a wedding, funeral, or naming ceremony expects patterns that respect the occasion.

This is a professional skill. Getting it wrong can lose a client permanently.

modules.title: Sierra Leonean pattern traditions
modules.content:
Sierra Leone has its own resist-dye traditions alongside the wider West African vocabulary. Common motifs include:

  • Concentric circles — representing continuity and the family
  • Zigzag lines — resilience, going around obstacles
  • Diamonds — prosperity and good fortune
  • Crosshatch — community and interconnection

Always ask the client what the cloth is for. Then choose motifs that match.

modules.title: Match the motif to the meaning

steps.q: Which motif is most appropriate for a naming ceremony?
steps.f: Concentric circles evoke continuity and family.

steps.q: A client commissions a cloth for a business launch. Best motif?
steps.f: Diamonds traditionally signal prosperity and good fortune.

steps.q: Which motif represents resilience and overcoming obstacles?
steps.f: Zigzags evoke going around or through obstacles — a resilience symbol.

modules.title: Commission for a memorial cloth
modules.prompt: A family commissions a Gara cloth to be draped at a memorial service. The deceased was a respected elder known for community service. Describe the pattern, colours, and any motif choices you would make — and why.
modules.context: Funeral textiles are one of the most important Gara commissions.
rubric: Uses colours appropriate to mourning (traditionally white and indigo, sometimes black)
Chooses motifs that reference community service or an elder's role
Explains the reasoning behind each choice
Considers asking the family about specific preferences
Avoids celebratory motifs inappropriate for the occasion

modules.title: Build a personal symbol library
modules.prompt: Compile a reference library of at least 10 traditional motifs with their meanings, drawn from elders, archives, or existing Gara work in your region.
steps: Interview at least 3 elder practitioners or visit a museum
Sketch each motif
Write a short note on its meaning and origin
Assemble into a reference document you can consult with clients

skillDomains.name: Dye Chemistry
skillDomains.description: The science behind the craft. Understand indigo, mordants, and pH.

skills.name: Indigo Fundamentals
skills.description: Work with natural indigo: prepare a vat, control pH, and produce consistent colour.

modules.title: What is indigo?
modules.content:
Indigo is a natural dye extracted from the leaves of Indigofera plants — grown throughout West Africa for centuries.

Indigo is unlike other dyes. It is not water-soluble in its natural form. To dye with it, you must chemically reduce it into a soluble yellow-green state, dye the cloth in that state, then expose it to air where it oxidises back to blue.

This is why freshly dyed indigo cloth looks green when it comes out of the vat and turns blue as it dries in the air.

modules.title: The indigo vat
modules.content:
Ingredients

  • Indigo powder
  • Water
  • Reducing agent (traditionally wood ash lye or ripe fruit; industrially, thiourea dioxide or sodium hydrosulfite)
  • Alkali (caustic soda or wood ash lye)

The process

  1. Dissolve indigo in warm water with a small amount of alkali.
  2. Add the reducing agent slowly.
  3. Wait. The vat will turn yellow-green with a coppery skin on top.
  4. It is ready when it smells slightly sweet and the skin is fully formed.

A healthy vat is a living thing. Feed it, warm it, and it produces colour for months.

steps.q: Your vat smells rotten and the cloth comes out grey, not blue. What's wrong?
o: The vat has gone off — too much organic matter, need to rebuild
steps.f: A rotten smell means bacterial contamination.

steps.q: The cloth comes out blue immediately without turning green first. What's happening?
o: The vat is not properly reduced
steps.f: If it doesn't come out yellow-green, the vat is not reduced.

steps.q: The colour is pale even after multiple dips. What's the most likely cause?
o: The vat is weak — low indigo concentration
steps.f: Pale colour means the vat needs more indigo.

modules.title: Achieve consistent colour across a batch
modules.prompt: You must dye 20 identical scarves to the same depth of indigo blue for a client order. Describe how you would ensure consistency across all 20 pieces.
modules.context: Consistency is the difference between artisan and industrial production.
rubric: Same vat for all pieces (not fresh per piece)
Same number of dips per piece
Same dip duration per piece
Same drying conditions
Batch documentation to track any variation

modules.title: Build an indigo depth swatch book
modules.prompt: Produce a swatch book of at least 6 shades of indigo, each achieved by a different number of dips in the same vat.
steps: Cut 6+ identical small squares of prepared cotton
Dye them in the same vat, one square per additional dip
Record dip count and duration
Dry all squares the same way
Mount them in order from lightest to darkest with the data alongside

skillDomains.name: Production & Finishing
skillDomains.description: Move from a single experiment to a repeatable production process.

skills.name: Batch Production
skills.description: Produce multiple identical or coordinated pieces at professional quality.

modules.title: One is a hobby. Ten is a business.
modules.content:
Making one beautiful cloth is a craft. Making ten identical beautiful cloths is a business.

Batch production requires:

  • A written process
  • Consistent materials
  • Timing discipline
  • Quality checkpoints

modules.title: Quality control checkpoints
modules.content:
Three checkpoints minimum

  1. Before dyeing — verify all fabric is identical, washed, and prepped. Verify the dye bath is at the target strength.
  2. During dyeing — verify each piece has been dipped the same number of times for the same duration.
  3. After drying — compare finished pieces side-by-side in daylight. Reject any that don't match.

Rejects are not wasted. They become practice pieces, apprentice learning material, or discounted stock.

steps.q: You're producing 20 pieces. When do you check the dye bath strength?
steps.f: Check bath strength before starting and again after every 5 pieces.

steps.q: Two finished pieces look different shades. What do you do?
o: Redip the lighter one or reject it
steps.f: Redip the lighter piece in the same vat.

steps.q: Final colour comparison between pieces should be done:
steps.f: Daylight, side by side is the only reliable comparison.

modules.title: Document a real production batch
modules.prompt: Produce a batch of at least 3 coordinated pieces (same design, same dye) and document the entire process.
steps: Choose a simple design you can repeat
Produce all 3 pieces in one session
Record every step in a notebook as you go
Photograph the finished batch together
Write a reflection: what varied? What would you change for a bigger batch?

skillDomains.name: Business & Market
skillDomains.description: Turn skill into income. Pricing, clients, and the realities of running a craft business.

skills.name: Pricing Your Work
skills.description: Price for survival, not just for the sale.

modules.title: The four-part price
modules.content:
Every price must cover four things:

  1. Materials — fabric, dye, thread, tools used up
  2. Labour — your time, at a real hourly rate
  3. Overhead — rent, water, electricity, transport
  4. Profit — the money that grows your business

Most beginners set price = materials + a little. That is why most beginners burn out.

Price = (Materials + Labour + Overhead) × (1 + Margin)

steps.q: Materials: 8,000 Le. Your time: 6 hours. Your hourly rate: 2,000 Le. Overhead per cloth: 1,000 Le. What is your base cost?
Base cost is 21,000 Le. You want a 30% margin. What's the price?
A client offers to pay you 20,000 for a cloth that costs 21,000 to make. What do you do?
steps.f: Accepting a loss teaches the client that your work is worth less than it costs.

modules.title: Price a commission
modules.prompt: A hotel commissions 15 identical Gara table runners. Materials are 12,000 Le each. You estimate 4 hours per piece at a rate of 2,500 Le/hour. Overhead is 800 Le per piece. You want a 35% margin. What is your final per-piece price, and how do you present it to the hotel?
modules.placeholder:
Base cost calculation:
Final price:
How I'll present it:
rubric: Correctly calculates base cost (materials + labour + overhead)
Correctly applies margin (multiplication, not addition)
Arrives at per-piece price
Proposes a professional presentation (itemised quote, not a bare number)
Addresses payment terms or deposit

modules.title: Raise your prices
modules.prompt: You've been selling Gara cloths at 30,000 Le. Your material costs have risen 20% this year. Write how you will communicate a price increase to your existing customers without losing them.
modules.context: Price increases are the hardest part of running a craft business.
rubric: Gives advance notice
Explains the reason (costs, not greed)
Frames the value the client receives
Offers a window to buy at old price for loyal customers
Holds the new price firmly once announced

modules.title: Build your professional rate card
modules.prompt: Create a one-page rate card listing your standard products and prices. Include sizes, materials, lead times, and payment terms.
steps: List your 3-5 standard products
Calculate the price for each using the four-part formula
Add realistic lead times based on your actual production speed
State deposit and payment terms
Design it cleanly — clients judge professionalism by presentation

skills.name: Finding Clients
skills.description: Sell without begging. Build a client base that returns and refers.

modules.title: Where clients come from
modules.content:
Clients come from six places, in order of reliability:

  1. Repeat customers — the cheapest client is the one you already have
  2. Referrals — happy clients tell others
  3. Local markets — direct selling, low barrier
  4. Boutiques and hotels — B2B, bigger orders
  5. Online — Instagram, WhatsApp Business, marketplaces
  6. Export — the highest reward, the highest effort

Beginners chase #5 and #6. Professionals build #1 and #2 first.

modules.title: WhatsApp Business as a sales tool
modules.content:
In West Africa, WhatsApp Business is the single most valuable free tool for a craft business. Here's how to use it professionally:

  • Set a clear business name and profile photo of your work
  • Write a short business description (one line, precise)
  • Create a catalogue with photos, descriptions, and prices
  • Use quick replies for common questions
  • Save every customer's name in your contacts with a label

A well-run WhatsApp Business account is worth more than most websites for a small craft business.

modules.title: Pitch a boutique
modules.prompt: You want to sell your Gara cloths to a Freetown boutique. Write the message you'll send them on WhatsApp. It should be under 150 words and include: who you are, what you make, why it fits their shop, and a clear next step.
modules.context: Cold outreach is a skill. Short, specific messages get responses.
rubric: Opens with a specific reason for contacting this boutique (not generic)
Describes what you make in one clear sentence
Explains why your work fits their shop
Includes a portfolio link or offer to visit
Ends with a specific ask (not 'let me know')

modules.title: Build your first client list
modules.prompt: Create a client tracking document with at least 10 potential buyers in your area (boutiques, hotels, wedding planners, or individual customers).
steps: Identify 10 real, specific potential clients
Record their names and contacts
For each, note one specific reason they'd want your work
Schedule a date to contact each one
Track responses in the same document
